prompt: A client asks about a feature's encryption details. The engineer isn't sure, says so, and promises an answer by tomorrow.
tells: isn't sure, says so, and promises an answer by tomorrow
why: Admit it and commit to finding out.
trap: There's no answer to put first.

prompt: In an interview, asked about a database feature they've never used, a candidate says they haven't used it and explains how they'd reason about it.
tells: says they haven't used it and explains how they'd reason about it

prompt: A junior PM gave an exec a made-up launch number to sound confident. Her mentor says next time to say she'll check and follow up within the hour.
tells: say she'll check and follow up within the hour
why: Guessing harms trust; admit and follow up.
trap: Following up is part of it, but the lesson is not bluffing.

prompt: Introduced as 'our AI expert', an engineer is asked about a legal question on model licenses. She says that's outside her expertise and names who would know.
tells: says that's outside her expertise and names who would know
why: Know the limits of your expertise.
trap: She isn't asking what it's for; she's admitting a limit.

prompt: At an all-hands, someone asks the CTO about layoffs rumors. He says he doesn't have that information yet and will share when he does.
tells: he doesn't have that information yet and will share when he does
why: Be honest about what you don't know.
trap: No feedback is being acted on.

prompt: Asked why latency doubled, the on-call says, 'I know it started at the deploy; I don't know the cause yet. Next update in 20 minutes.'
tells: I don't know the cause yet
why: Separate what you know from what you don't.
trap: It's short, but the key is admitting the unknown.
